Pleterje
PLEH-ter-yeh
n. (the Slovenian charterhouse of 1407, the only Carthusian house still living in the Slavic lands)
From Slovene pleter, wickerwork or a plaited fence.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Pleterje in Lower Carniola was founded in 1407 by Count Hermann II of Celje and was the last of the four Carthusian houses of the Slovene lands. It was abandoned in 1595 under Turkish pressure and the buildings decayed for three centuries; only the Gothic church of 1420 survived more or less whole. Carthusians returned in 1899, rebuilt the cloister and cells, and the house is the only living charterhouse in the Slavic world; its orchards and brandy support it. This dictionary records Pleterje for the single surviving church, because what remains when most is lost is one of Scripture's own governing ideas and it has a name. A remnant is left by God's doing, “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant” (Isa 1:9). It is preserved on a specific principle, “Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5). It is said to be small and to be enough, “a remnant shall be saved” (Rom 9:27), and it is described as putting out roots again, “out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant” (2Ki 19:31).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a remnant as that which is left; a residue as the remainder; to preserve as to keep from injury; desolate as laid waste; and election as the choice of some to eternal life.

expand to see more

REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part; the small part that remains.

RESIDUE, n. That which remains after a part is taken, separated, removed or designated; remainder; rest.

PRESERVE, v.t. To keep or save from injury or destruction; to defend from evil; to uphold; to save from decay.

DESOLATE, adj. Destitute or deprived of inhabitants; laid waste; in a ruinous condition; neglected; left alone.

ELECTION, n. In theology, divine choice; predetermination of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy.

Key Scripture

Isa 1:9 — "Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah."

Rom 11:5 — "Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace."

Rom 9:27 — "Esaias also crieth concerning Israel, Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved:"

2Ki 19:31 — "For out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, and they that escape out of mount Zion: the zeal of the LORD of hosts shall do this."

Modern Corruption

Slovenian charterhouse of 1407: abandoned under Turkish pressure, its Gothic church alone surviving three centuries, and monks back since 1899.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a remnant in Scripture is never an accident of attrition. Isaiah traces the survival of anything at all to God's act and says what the alternative was, “we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah” (Isa 1:9). Paul takes the word up and attaches it to a doctrine rather than to a demographic, “there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5).

The second thing is that smallness is not treated as failure. Paul quotes Isaiah on a people as numerous as the sand of the sea and a salvation confined to a remnant, “a remnant shall be saved” (Rom 9:27), and Hezekiah is promised a remnant that will go out and take root again, “out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant” (2Ki 19:31). One roofed church among ruins for three hundred years, and then a community again, is what the word looks like in masonry.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sarid (H8300), a survivor; Greek leimma (G3005), a remnant; Greek ekloge (G1589), election; Hebrew pelet (H6413), an escape; Hebrew she'ar (H7605), a remainder.

expand to see more

Hebrew sarid (H8300) — a survivor, left by God; “had left unto us a very small remnant”, Isaiah 1:9.

Greek leimma (G3005) — a remnant, what is left over; “there is a remnant according to the election of grace”, Romans 11:5.

Greek ekloge (G1589) — election, choosing out; “according to the election of grace”, Romans 11:5.

Greek kataleimma (G2640) — a residue that shall be saved; “a remnant shall be saved”, Romans 9:27.

Hebrew she'ar (H7605) — a remainder going forth; “out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant”, 2 Kings 19:31.

Usage

"“had left unto us a very small remnant” (Isa 1:9) — survival traced to God's act."

"“according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5) — a doctrine, not a demographic."

"“out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant” (2Ki 19:31) — small, and sent out again."
